newsitem.title: FRANCE: Court intrigue, insect passion, grab French awards.
newsitem.headline: Court intrigue, insect passion, grab French awards.

text.p: Sexual intrigue and humiliation in "Ridicule", together with insect-scale passion and murder in "Microcosmos", dominated the French Oscars at this weekend's glitzy award ceremony.

The French film industry handed its Cesar prize for best film late on Saturday to Patrice Leconte's lavishly-costumed "Ridicule", which tracks a low-ranking nobleman's doomed efforts to make good in the Versailles palace of Louis XVI.

The film also won awards for best decor, best costumes, and best director -- shared with Bernard Tavernier for "Capitaine Conan". Fanny Ardant, suave and calculating but ultimately ridiculed in "Ridicule", took the best actress award but for another performance, in the comedy "Pedale Douce".

Leconte, whose latest offering launched the Cannes Film Festival last year, has tried his hand at a host of different genres but is best-known for bringing teams of actors from Paris cafe-theatres to the silver screen, as in the hit 1970s comedy "Les Bronzes" (The Holidaymakers).
The microscopic cast of stylish documentary "Microcosmos", also hailed in Cannes, grabbed as many as five Cesars for best photography, best editing, best sound, best music and best producer.

Directed by the French couple Claude Nuridsany and Marie Perennou, who are both biologists and photographers, "Microcosmos" follows the lives of the seven-dot Ladybird, the Rhinoceros beetle and the Bourgogne snails among others.
Sex, violence and cannibalism all feature in the movie -- the snails hold each other tight in a sexual embrace, two Rhinoceros beetles lock their tiny horns in a territorial battle on a twig.

The best foreign film award went to "Breaking the Waves" by Danish maverick Lars von Trier, an alluring melodrama pitting the elders who rule a remote Scottish fishing village against an apparently naive young girl and her tortured relationship with her paralysed husband.
